book: 184 - The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life

chapters.relation: Kraft uses Dunder Mifflin to test whether stockholder profit or stakeholder welfare should drive business decisions, introducing stakeholder theory via Ansoff and the Mitchell salience model. Michael's exclusive patronage of national chains (Chili's, Starbucks, USA Today) versus the staff's loyalty to local spots like Poor Richard's becomes a Millian case: by Mill's point that most good action benefits particular individuals, shopping locally spreads happiness through the Scranton community while Michael's habits export money and decision-making elsewhere. Dwight oscillates between stockholder logic (the cheapest health plan, poaching Jim's client in 'Diversity Day') and stakeholder-minded customer service, while 'Halloween,' 'Health Care,' and 'Branch Closing' show profit trumping people; Michael's successful sale to Christian at Chili's in 'The Client' balances both, and his 'Show me that farm' speech insists workers like Stanley and Phyllis are not replaceable cogs.

Johnson works through the standard objections to affirmative action using Scranton material: Ryan's paralysis before the all-Black management team in 'Traveling Salesmen' shows a single-race workforce is not intrinsically bad, while Michael's Chris Rock routine and his do-it-yourself slur exercise in 'Diversity Day' show that Dunder Mifflin meeting every quota does nothing about racism. A hypothetical about Dwight's grandfather refusing to hire Stanley's grandfather at the beet farm frames the compensation objection, answered by the 'cycle of poverty' account of the present effects of past discrimination. Finally, a fictitious hiring of guard Hank Tate over a better-qualified white candidate - justified, following Nagel, by the consequences of calming branch unrest - sets up the conclusion that education, not racially preferential hiring, would break minority poverty without discrimination, so affirmative action is ultimately unjustified.

Nys asks whether political correctness is a genuine moral demand or mere verbal hygiene, using the British Office: Gareth's racist BMC joke, Brent aborting it when Oliver the Black coworker arrives, the 'wanking claw' impression, and the porn email with Brent's head pasted onto a woman's body. He argues words genuinely wound (Brent's 'sticks and stones' rehearsal collapses when Gareth reveals his cruel nicknames) but that offense is wrong as disrespect for human equality rather than as a feeling, an account filled out with Frankfurt's claim that our identity depends on what we care about, so the non-targeted can be offended too. After weighing Mill's defense of free discussion for social progress, the pornography debate (in which reduction to body parts is exactly what degrades, as Brent complains he was 'objectified'), and Marx's notion of ideology as a concealing set of ideas behind a 'white male' bias, he concludes that Brent's flaw is looking good rather than being good, and that PC language is rhetorical make-up over persisting inequality.

Dromm asks what makes Michael's behavior wrong even where the law cannot touch it: as an 'equal-opportunity harasser' of Pam, Ryan, and Oscar, Michael seems to escape Title VII's discrimination requirement. He tests Edmund Wall's 'wrongful communication' definition against the filthy emails, 'that's what she said,' and Michael's solution to the Kevin-Angela dispute in 'Conflict Resolution,' finds it too broad and too dependent on the victim's objection, then turns to MacKinnon's sex-discrimination account and Crosthwaite and Priest's oppression account to explain the distinctive harm to women (pressuring Pam to be a cheerleader in 'Basketball,' calling the party-planning committee his 'bitches'). He concludes that both views are needed, and that in the end harassment wrongs workers by undermining their legitimate expectation of being judged only on job-relevant merit, leaving Dwight's extra effort done for nothing.

Johnson asks what Dunder Mifflin morally owes after the obscene watermark scandal in 'Product Recall': stockholder theory says only refund and apologize insofar as that protects the bottom line, while stakeholder theory demands real amends to Barbara Allen and the Dunmore High prom attendees even at a profit cost. He then argues corporate responsibility cannot attach to a mindless company, and builds a criterion of blameworthiness - failing to do what it is one's job to do when that failure causally contributes to the incident - which convicts Creed (skipping his weekly mill quality checks all year), Michael (never verifying the inspections happened, despite his 'escape goat' apology video), and Jan (retaining an incompetent manager), all of whom should have been fired.

Arp and Watson sort Dunder Mifflin's relationships into five conceptions of love: Roy's erotic 'best sex of your life' Valentine's offer to Pam as blind eros; Angela and Dwight's pursuit of an idealized mate read through Plato's Forms and the Symposium's ascent to Beauty; Aristotle's three friendships, under which the office's alliances are mere utility while Jim and Pam's teapot sacrifice in 'Christmas Party' approaches virtue friendship; the Stoic-Kantian 'equal loving' of universal respect, laughed at when Michael ranks himself with Bono and Lincoln; and agape-style family loyalty that leads Dwight to supply Michael his urine in 'Drug Testing'. The chapter concludes that Michael exemplifies a selfishness Western philosophy has no name for, failing at every form of love.

Nys uses Brent's quiz grievance about Mr. Spock (half-Vulcan, half-human) and his Crufts pedigree-dog analogy, Gareth's 'look at the ears' classification test, the dwarf/midget/elf/pixie interrogation of Alex, and Tim and Dawn's 'lethal blow' prank to introduce the problem of natural kinds. Realist answers come from Kripke (water is H2O whatever we call it), Aristotle's matter-and-form essences, and the DNA evidence separating Bornean clouded leopards from mainland cousins, while Wittgenstein's language games and Quine's point that our innate similarity senses mislead support the constructivist that we lay classification on an unstructured world. The verdict: nature supplies real differences but never carves itself into kinds, and the line-drawing remains up to us.

Luck defends Gareth's announcement that he 'knows no one is present' when Tim hides behind his wall of files: since Tim's presence is a fifty-fifty gamble, the Rule of Acceptance (believe only what is more likely than not) plus the Conjunction Principle commit Gareth to believing Tim both present and absent, so announcing is the only act consistent with both beliefs. A Brent-style redundancy lottery - rationally believing of each of thirty employees that they will not be fired while knowing someone must be - shows the same tolerable inconsistency, and the chapter concludes, following Graham Priest, that Gareth is an unwitting practitioner of paraconsistent logic.

Mayock runs theories of the self through the Scranton cast: Michael's burned foot in 'The Injury' enacts materialism, corrected by Aristotle's and Aquinas's distinction between accidental and substantial change; Jim's chair-and-phone role-play in 'Halloween' and his Dwight impersonation in 'Product Recall' ('Identity theft is not a joke') illustrate qualitative versus numerical identity and Descartes's cogito and dualism; Dwight's obsession with upgrading 'Assistant (to the) Regional Manager' is an ontological-status crisis met by Nietzsche's claim that the 'I' is a grammatical fiction and Hume's bundle theory. The chapter lands on Hegel's recognition - the self exists only in being acknowledged - reading Michael's office family, the Prodigal Son greetings, and his need for Pam to decode Jan's message as social constructionism in action.

Lonergan and Wisnewski read 'Grief Counseling' and 'Safety Training' as a case study in death-denial: Michael cannot parse the euphemism 'we lost Ed Truck,' Kelly must teach him to be sad, and Creed's report of the decapitation forces the Heideggerian realization that death is his own not-to-be-outstripped possibility, not just a fact of life. The office deflects with movie plots and euphemism (Jim's 'seriously hurt' about the rooftop stunt), Pam's eulogy for Toby's bird shows how mourning ritual copes with mortality, and Michael's longing to be remembered - hospital wings named after him, saving his own life - exemplifies Kierkegaard's 'world-historical' life as an ego defense, with living subjectively the recommended but unexplained alternative. Becker's thesis that all culture is a fabricated protest against death frames the whole chapter.

Written as a fake email thread among University of Scranton faculty, the appendix has junior professor Joe Kraus propose reading the town through Baudrillard's simulacrum - the 'Scranton Welcomes You' sign from the credits becoming real for him only as a TV image - while senior colleagues tutor him through the history of representation theory. Stephen deploys Plato's Ion (Socrates' magnet-and-iron chain of imitation, with Ion's Brent-like obliviousness) and Aristotle on mimesis, pity, fear, and catharsis to explain the show's tragicomic discomfort, while Maria adds the Antiochene, Alexandrian, and Augustinian fourfold senses of scripture applied to Scranton; Michael Friedman contributes a Chekhovian reading of Pam's bird eulogy as subtext about Michael's fear of dying alone. The thread itself mirrors an Office plotline as the senior faculty quietly decide to cut the untenured Joe out of the project.

This appendix compiles Dwight's talking-head 'facts' episode by episode through season four - his beet farm and volunteer sheriff's deputy credentials, the Assistant (to the) Regional Manager obsession, Schrute Bucks, the resorbed twin, shunning, bear lore, and recorder performances - followed by entries from his blog. It advances no philosophical argument and engages no philosopher; its role in the volume is to supply, in Dwight's own deadpan and self-contradictory idiom, the raw character material that the book's chapters on identity, classification, and workplace ethics draw on.

holes.name: Stakeholder Theory
holes.what: The business-ethics view that a firm's decisions must weigh everyone affected by them - employees, customers, suppliers, the community - rather than only stockholder profit.
holes.why: Chapter 25 (and again chapter 29) is organized around weighing stakeholder theory against stockholder-first management at Dunder Mifflin, and no taxonomy slug covers it.

holes.name: Affirmative Action
holes.what: Preferential policies (quotas, set-asides, minority preference in hiring) designed to remedy the present effects of past discrimination.
holes.why: Chapter 26's entire argument about whether affirmative action is justified, and whether education could replace it, turns on this concept, which the taxonomy lacks.

holes.name: Political Correctness (offensive speech)
holes.what: The debate over whether language and jokes that demean groups are wrong as disrespect for equality, and whether free speech or offense-avoidance should govern them.
holes.why: Chapter 27 is wholly about political (in)correctness in The Office - racist jokes, slurs, and porn at work - a topic with no matching taxonomy slug.

holes.name: Sexual Harassment
holes.what: Unwelcome sexual or gender-directed workplace conduct, analyzed either as wrongful communication violating privacy and autonomy or as discrimination that maintains women's subordination.
holes.why: Chapter 28 is entirely devoted to defining what makes Michael Scott a sexual harasser and why it is wrong, a concept absent from the taxonomy.

holes.name: Shareholder Primacy (Stockholder Theory)
holes.what: Milton Friedman's view that a manager's sole moral obligation is to spend stockholders' money maximizing profit, from which no unprofitable good deeds are required.
holes.why: Chapter 29 states and then attacks this stockholder argument before endorsing stakeholder amends for the watermark scandal; Friedman himself is also absent from the taxonomy.

holes.name: Moral Responsibility and Blameworthiness
holes.what: The conditions under which an agent deserves blame for an outcome - classically requiring intentional causation, here refined to failing a job duty that causally contributed to the harm.
holes.why: Chapter 29 builds a criterion of blameworthiness to decide who should be fired for the watermark incident (Creed, Michael, Jan), a core ethics concept the taxonomy lacks.

holes.name: Natural Kinds
holes.what: The question of whether the world is objectively carved into kinds (water, leopards, species) that our terms track, or whether classification is a human convention imposed on unstructured reality.
holes.why: Chapter 32 is organized entirely around the natural-kinds debate introduced by Brent's Mr. Spock and dwarf/midget/elf classifications; no taxonomy slug covers it.

holes.name: Paraconsistent Logic (dialetheism)
holes.what: A non-classical logic that rejects the Law of Non-Contradiction and the Principle of Explosion, allowing rational reasoning from inconsistent premises (as in the lottery/redundancy paradox).
holes.why: Chapter 33 argues Gareth's 'Case of the Missing Tim' announcement is rational precisely because it reasons paraconsistently; the taxonomy has no logic concepts at all.

holes.name: Graham Priest
holes.what: Contemporary logician (b. 1948) and leading champion of paraconsistency and dialetheism, author of 'The Logic of Paradox'.
holes.why: Chapter 33 explicitly follows the 'cause of paraconsistency' led most notably by Priest to defend Gareth's rationality.

holes.name: Ernest Becker
holes.what: Cultural anthropologist (1924-1974) whose The Denial of Death argues that terror of mortality secretly motivates all culture and human activity.
holes.why: Chapter 35 uses Becker's death-denial thesis as its master framework for Michael's grief over Ed Truck, the bird funeral, and the rooftop stunt.

holes.name: The Denial of Death
holes.what: The repressive strategy of treating death as a mere fact of life that happens to others, through euphemism, ritual, and quests for symbolic immortality.
holes.why: Chapter 35 diagnoses every character - Michael above all - as denying death rather than confronting it, a concept distinct from Heidegger's being-toward-death and absent from the taxonomy.

holes.name: Mimesis (art as imitation)
holes.what: The theory that art imitates reality - for Plato twice removed from the Forms and knowledge-free, for Aristotle a natural instinct whose tragedy arouses pity and fear to produce catharsis.
holes.why: Chapter 36 runs from Baudrillard back through Plato's Ion and Aristotle's Poetics precisely to frame The Office as an imitation of Scranton, and the taxonomy has no mimesis or catharsis slug.
